report.source_text: An X-ray of the neck and a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck and chest revealed that the retropharyngeal air and mediastinal emphysema were completely resolved, with no evidence of soft tissue air nor any fluid collection (Figures 3, 4).

clinician.final_diagnosis: a spontaneous esophageal rupture in the absence of any precipitating factors
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 20-year-old female presented with sudden retrosternal chest pain, radiating to the neck, throat pain, difficulty swallowing, voice change, and shortness of breath. Initial chest X-ray revealed air in the mediastinum (E001). A CT scan of the neck and chest confirmed retropharyngeal air extending to the mediastinum with anterior chest surgical emphysema, with no definite foreign body (E002). Despite these findings, subsequent Gastrografin and Barium studies (esophagram) were reported as 'insignificant' (E005), and an upper endoscopy (OGD) revealed only mild gastritis with no evidence of foreign body or injury to the esophagus (E003). The patient denied any history of foreign body ingestion, vomiting, trauma, or recent procedures. On the next day, all her symptoms subsided (E004). One week post-discharge, follow-up X-ray of the neck and contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck and chest showed complete resolution of the retropharyngeal air and mediastinal emphysema, with no evidence of soft tissue air or fluid collection (E006). The overall clinical picture, including initial imaging findings, spontaneous symptom resolution, and resolution of air on follow-up, supports a self-limiting spontaneous esophageal rupture, despite negative direct visualization tests.
